The Director-General of the Nigerian Institute of Medical Research, Prof. John Obafunwa, has disclosed that Nigeria still sends too many biological samples abroad for sequencing because of inadequate local capacity. Obafunwa made the disclosure at the opening of the Institute’s 2026 Annual International Science Week Conference in Lagos, while calling for increased investment in research infrastructure and scientific manpower. He also revealed that financial constraints had stalled the establishment of a major laboratory complex planned for 2025. Speaking on the theme, “Health Research in the Era of Advanced Technology,” the DG said that although artificial intelligence, genomics and other technological advances were changing medical research, Nigeria must develop the infrastructure and expertise required to benefit from them. He said, “Health data from Nigerian patients and samples is a national asset,” stressing that such information must be collected ethically, secured, and used for the benefit of communities. He urged government, policymakers and development partners to invest in laboratories, computing facilities, data systems and human capacity. The DG also challenged researchers to move beyond generating scientific findings to ensuring that discoveries translate into practical interventions for patients. Earlier, the Conference Chairman, Dr Tunji Olowolafe, said Nigeria should already have the capacity to produce its own vaccines. African scientists target stomach ulcers, cancer with homegrown solutions Medical practitioners need business skills to fix healthcare — Stakeholders Pathology not all about dead bodies, says NIMR DG Olowolafe, the Chancellor of Ekiti State University, said the country should possess the laboratories, expertise and infrastructure needed to investigate emerging diseases and respond to outbreaks without excessive dependence on external support. He commended NIMR for its contributions during the Ebola crisis and COVID-19 pandemic, adding that local research institutions must play a central role in the country’s ambition to produce medicines and vaccines. He said government initiatives aimed at strengthening local pharmaceutical and vaccine production must be supported by credible research institutions. In the keynote address, the Chief Medical Director of Lagos State University Teaching Hospital, Prof Adetokunbo Fabanwo, represented by Prof Adebowale Adekoya, said scientific discoveries must be translated into clinical interventions capable of improving patient outcomes and reducing mortality. He identified artificial intelligence, genomic medicine, molecular diagnostics, robotics, telemedicine and 3D printing as technologies that could improve diagnosis, treatment and healthcare delivery. However, he warned that the high cost of technology, inadequate infrastructure, shortage of trained personnel and insufficient funding could prevent Nigerians from benefiting from these innovations. He called for dedicated funding for implementation research, stronger collaboration among universities, teaching hospitals and industries, and the establishment of translational research centres. The conference, which brought together researchers, clinicians, policymakers and students, is focused on exploring how emerging technologies can strengthen health research and healthcare delivery in Nigeria.
